sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Determinants as Area
sections.content: Briefly recall that the determinant of a 2x2 matrix represents the signed area of the parallelogram formed by its column vectors. Explain that if the area is zero, the vectors are linearly dependent (collapsed).
sections.example: Visualizing a unit square being stretched into a parallelogram by a transformation matrix.

sections.title: Framing the Linear System
sections.content: Represent the system Ax = b as a vector equation: x1(v1) + x2(v2) = b, where v1 and v2 are column vectors of A. Geometrically, this means finding the linear combination of v1 and v2 that reaches the point b.
sections.example: A robot arm (represented by vectors v1 and v2) trying to reach a specific coordinate point b in 2D space.

sections.title: Geometric Interpretation of Cramer's Rule
sections.content: Explain that replacing a column of A with vector b creates a new parallelogram. Show that the ratio of the area of this new parallelogram to the original determinant is exactly the scaling factor x_i.
sections.example: Use two overlapping parallelograms: the original base (Area=det(A)) and the 'b-replaced' version. As b shifts, the shadow/area changes proportionally.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Visualization
sections.content: Animate the process: 1. Calculate Area(A). 2. Swap column 1 with b. 3. Calculate Area(A1). 4. Reveal x1 = Area(A1) / Area(A). Explain the intuition: we are comparing the 'volume' contribution of each vector.
sections.example: A character 'Scaling Sally' adjusting the length of her vector components to fill the target 'Area b' perfectly.

sections.title: Summary and Limitations
sections.content: Conclude that Cramer's rule is a geometric ratio. Mention that while elegant, it is computationally expensive (n!) for large systems, suitable mostly for small, intuitive problems.
sections.example: Compare the 'geometric insight' of Cramer's Rule to the 'brute force' efficiency of Gaussian Elimination using a simple balance scale metaphor.
